title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a training-data sourcing problem. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius as specific scraping sources. That data collection happened before deployment, meaning any copyright problem baked into the training set was carried forward into every piece of music the system later generated for users.

The second failure is at the output layer. When record labels prompted both Suno and Udio with targeted requests, the systems reproduced recognizable portions of specific copyrighted songs, including close imitations of Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." This is a model reproducing training material rather than generating novel output, and it occurred in a publicly deployed product with no apparent filtering to catch near-copies of known works before they reached users. A rights-clearance review at the training stage, or an output similarity check at deployment, would have been the points at which this could have been caught.

What is not established: the lawsuits and class actions are allegations, not verdicts, and while a German court ruled against Suno in the GEMA case, the US litigation remains unresolved at the time of reporting. Settlements between Suno and Warner Music Group, and between Udio and Universal Music, were reached, but the terms and any admissions of liability are not detailed in the available reporting.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse these companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission to train their models and of directly reproducing sections of famous songs in their AI-generated outputs. The record labels submitted a lengthy list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were used for training, featuring catalogs from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Frank Sinatra, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels tested both AI music generators using specific prompts and demonstrated that they could repeatedly recreate versions of famous copyrighted songs. For example, they generated AI music that closely mimicked Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and created a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and in Massachusetts against Suno, setting up a significant court battle over how generative AI services should handle copyrighted material across music, art, video, and text.
